# Report on "Helicobacter Connections" (Marshall, Nobel Lecture 2005)

## 1. The question, frozen
The lecture answers several questions: what causes peptic ulcer, how the discovery was made, and how it was resisted. The title and opening make the *cause* central — "the title … refers to the two components of our discovery: we were able to associate a new bacterium with peptic ulcer disease." So I freeze the causal question:

**What causes peptic ulcer, over the range of adult ulcer patients, and what can we read off from seeing the bacterium?** Forward question (what produces it), with a backward tail (what a biopsy or antibody test tells us). Range left out and later pulled in: childhood, gastric cancer, non-ulcer dyspepsia. I flag those when they move.

## 2. The explanation in parts
- P1 The bacterium is present in the stomach of ulcer patients, and is not a harmless bystander.
- P2 It causes chronic gastritis.
- P3 It is a genuine pathogen: swallowing a culture gave a healthy man gastritis (the self-experiment).
- P4 It is picked up in early childhood and persists for life, giving lifelong susceptibility.
- P5 It survives acid by making urease and hiding in mucus.
- P6 Eradicating it with antibiotics cures the ulcer; bismuth heals partly by killing it.
- P7 The old rivals — stress, personality, smoking, excess acid — are effects or bystanders, not the cause.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Held by / why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 bacterium in ulcers | **Held** | 13/13 duodenal ulcers; removing it leaves the association unexplained |
| P2 gastritis from the bacterium | **Held** | biopsy data; bismuth heals the gastritis |
| P3 it is a pathogen | **Held (built)** | the self-ingestion poke: cause introduced, effect appears |
| P4 caught in childhood, lifelong | **Held if** | held only by the "no remembered acute illness" job, itself resting on a re-reading of old literature |
| P5 urease / acid survival | **Held** | remove it and acid survival is unexplained (though the lab first scored it urease-negative — a data fault, not the part) |
| P6 antibiotics cure | **Held** | double-blind trial, relapse curves; the strongest part |
| P7 old causes are effects | **Held** | smoking stopped mattering once the bacterium was gone |
| name/taxonomy (Campylobacter → Helicobacter) | **Loose** | any of several would do; a convention |
| "anything you might swallow" corrodes the stomach (NSAID ulcers) | **Catch-all, with a partial gauge** | gauge: NSAID history and normal histology |
| gastric cancer link | **Held if** | asserted in 1983, supported by later epidemiology, not tested here |
| "ulcer personality" is a result, not a cause | **Borrowed** | rests on the chronic-infection explanation, not tested in the trial |
| Marshall's own infection clearing by itself | **Unknown** | he says a mystery; test would be a follow-up study of untreated early infection |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks
**Change list.** What the claim covers: give antibiotics vs. acid-lowering drugs; eradicate the bacterium; look at people who never got it. Changes it leaves out: how it spreads (faecal–oral, asserted), who among the infected gets an ulcer, the NSAID cases. The first is stated; the third is quietly handled by the catch-all.

**Flip.** Had ulcers lacked the bacterium, the theory fails. It risked a great deal and survived, including the one apparent exception (the negative duodenal-ulcer patient, reassigned after the surgical specimen showed bacteria — a patch worth watching, but consistent with the data).

**Direction.** Passes the hard test. Poking the cause (the self-experiment; antibiotics) moves the effect. Poking the effect (surgery for a bleeding ulcer) does not move the bacterium. This is why the lecture's causal claim is not the old backward reading ("ulcer patients happen to carry bacteria").

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** The old rival did this: "ulcer comes from stress and excess acid" just renamed the thing to be explained. Marshall's account has a mild version — "pathogen" and "the immune system treats it as one" (the antibody test) leans on the conclusion. What rescues it is the mechanism work (urease, mucus, childhood acquisition, gastritis), which is not the conclusion under another name.

**Pairs that pull.** The sharpest: **43% of healthy donors carry it, yet most never get an ulcer.** The theory needs a part explaining who converts susceptibility into disease. "Lifelong susceptibility, sometimes punctuated by ulcer" is where this joint is loose. Second pair: bismuth (a "free"/inherited old remedy) is pulled into service as an antibiotic; the pull is resolved by the in-vitro disc test.

**Rivals.** The stress/acid theory and the bacterial theory are told apart by a change on the list: bismuth's lower relapse rate, and antibiotic cure. So this is not a case of "the same explanation at this level" — the difference is real and checkable. Good.

**Where the parts came from.** P1, P2, P6 are **fitted** to the 100-patient series and the trial. P3 is **built** (a designed poke). P4 and the gastric-cancer link are closer to **asserted**/re-read — the "suddenly the whole process became clear" synthesis. P5 borrows from acid physiology and Koch's postulates as background.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary
Two moves tighten it most: (a) give P4 (childhood acquisition) an independent test — follow children prospectively, not re-read old epidemics; (b) supply the missing part that says why most infected people never ulcerate (strain, host, or timing). Without (b), the "susceptibility" word is doing quiet work.

## 6. What this does not show
Passing is not truth. Most of the lecture's claims about the past (childhood, cancer, transmission) are told with hindsight and could pass while being partly wrong; several are marked "held if" or "unknown" above. The lecture is also a self-account, so some parts are shaped to credit the discoverer.

## 7. One next step
Name and run the test that would settle P4: does early childhood infection, tracked forward, predict later ulcer? If yes, the loose joint closes; if not, that part was fitted to old stories.
